description: We are looking for creative and curious individuals with skills in design, programming, engineering, or space science to join our team and help develop our project.
summary:
Our software project is called Space Eddus. It is a health monitoring platform designed to help astronauts stay healthy during space missions, where access to medical care is limited and even small changes in the body can become serious.
Developed in Python using Streamlit, Plotly, and SQLite, the platform combines scientific research on human physiology with real space weather data from NASA and NOAA.
Space Eddus learns each crew member's personal health baseline and continues monitoring them throughout the mission. It focuses on three major health risks: muscle loss and malnutrition, sleep cycle disruption, and hidden infections. It also monitors urgent threats such as radiation storms, low oxygen levels, cortisol levels, and dangerous changes in blood glucose.
When it detects unusual changes, the system calculates a 0–100 Operational Readiness Score, adjusts monitoring schedules and provides medical recommendations. Astronauts can track their health and treatments, while flight surgeons can monitor the crew, review alerts, adjust prescriptions, and make informed medical decisions remotely.
Our goal is to make healthcare more accessible in space,and to protect astronauts during long missions.
details:
Space Eddus is an autonomous health-monitoring platform that spots medical problems early in astronauts on long missions. The software establishes a personalized physiological baseline for each astronaut at the beginning of the mission. After that, it checks every day for Z-score deviations across smartwatch vitals, sleep stages, body composition from bioimpedance, capillary blood glucose, hemoglobin, salivary biomarkers sampled through the day, menstrual cycle records, and space radiation doses.

The platform runs on 17 physiological models. With them it tracks three major spaceflight risks: muscle loss and malnutrition, circadian and HPA-axis misalignment, and hidden early infection. It also watches acute safety limits for glucose, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, and solar particle storms. From all of this, it produces a 0–100 Operational Readiness Score, a three-level traffic-light status, and step-by-step medical action plans. 

The main benefit is that crews can manage their health proactively and on their own when distance and communication delays make real-time help from Earth impossible. To keep astronauts from being flooded with minor warnings, yellow alerts are grouped into one daily report, while red alerts fire immediately for true emergencies. A red alert also switches the astronaut to an intensive sampling schedule that saves medical supplies and crew time. 

We built the platform in Python 3.11+, using SQLite for local storage with custom repository and Unit-of-Work patterns. The interface uses Streamlit, Plotly, custom CSS, and Figma prototypes. To tie space weather monitoring to real orbital conditions, the backend pulls live solar flare, CME, SEP, and proton flux data from NASA CCMC DONKI and NOAA SWPC. It caches those events locally, so the software keeps working fully offline. To keep the code clean, the medicine accurate, and deployment dependable, we rely on 163 automated unit, integration, and UI tests in pytest, PEP 8 linting with ruff, Git/GitHub for version control, and hosting on Streamlit Community Cloud.

One of Space Eddus’s most creative features is its emergency simulator, which is grounded in physiology. Flight surgeons can copy real telemetry into an isolated simulation layer, inject realistic clinical events such as a fever that decouples from heart rate, or a blunted cortisol awakening response; and then roll the scenario back cleanly, leaving the astronaut’s historical baseline untouched. Throughout development, our team focused on clinical specificity, privacy, and modular architecture. The infection engine avoids false positives by requiring both a temperature deviation and a second autonomic sign, and it adjusts for the luteal-phase temperature rise in female astronauts. Authentication runs locally with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512 and brute-force lockout, so biometric records never depend on an outside identity provider. And a strict separation between pure clinical math, data services, and UI views keeps the code easy to maintain.
